article.title: 4 Supply Categories
article.author: Sejal Desai
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Peak sales periods expose weaknesses in packaging and shipping setups. A slightly inadequate box or a mailing bag that tears occasionally is a minor annoyance at 20 orders a day. When they blew up to 200 orders a day during Black Friday or the Christmas rush, that same small problem multiplied into a genuine customer service and cost issue. Box and Mailer Sizing Across the Product Range Businesses start with a handful of box sizes that cover their initial product range and never revisit that setup as the range expands. Products that don’t fit well into existing box options end up shipped in oversized boxes with excess void fill. They may also be squeezed into boxes that are technically too small. Both of which increase damage risk and shipping costs. Reviewing eCommerce Shipping Supplies against the current product catalogue reveals gaps. For example, a new product line that’s slightly larger might be getting packed inefficiently in every shipment. The same can be said for those with different shapes. That inefficiency compounds once order volume spikes during peak periods. Void Fill Stock Levels and Type Void fill runs out faster than most businesses expect once volume increases, and running short during a peak period means staff either scrambling to source more urgently at higher cost, or shipping products with inadequate protection because that’s what’s available at the time. This is also worth reviewing for type, not just quantity. Air pillows work well for lightweight items but don’t provide much protection for heavier or fragile products, where paper fill or foam might be more appropriate. Checking that the void fill type actually matches what’s being protected matters more once order volume means less time for staff to make judgment calls on individual packages. Tape, Labels, and the Consumables That Run Out Silently Packing tape, shipping labels, and thermal printer supplies are the kind of consumables that get ordered reactively, someone notices the tape’s running low and places an order, usually with enough lead time during normal months. During peak periods, consumption increases dramatically, and the same reactive ordering pattern that worked fine in July can leave a warehouse without tape or labels for a day or two in December, right when order volume is at its highest. Checking current stock levels against realistic peak period order volume, not just current daily usage, and placing orders with enough lead time before the rush actually starts, avoids the scramble of trying to source labels or tape urgently when every supplier is dealing with the same seasonal demand spike. Return Packaging and Processing Supplies Peak sales periods generate peak return periods a few weeks later, and this is the category most businesses forget to plan for until returns start arriving. If the business includes prepaid return labels or return packaging with outbound shipments, stock for this needs to scale alongside outbound packaging, not get reviewed separately or overlooked entirely. Even businesses that don’t include return materials upfront need enough packaging on hand to process returns efficiently once they start arriving, repackaging returned items for restocking, or preparing them for return to suppliers if that’s part of the process. A returns backlog caused by inadequate supplies creates a slower restocking cycle, which affects inventory availability for the next wave of sales right when a business needs stock moving quickly.
